summary: Park Medi World operates the Park Hospitals network, providing consultations, tests, hospital stays, procedures and specialist care.
description: A patient may visit a doctor and leave the same day, or be admitted for a stay and treatment. Park provides the teams, beds, equipment, nursing and support needed for the services available at each hospital. A building alone cannot provide care: qualified people and functioning facilities must be in place.
money: The hospital bills for delivered consultations, tests, stays, procedures and related services. A patient or family may pay directly, or an insurer, employer or healthcare scheme may pay under an agreement. Doctors, nurses, medicines, supplies, equipment and premises must be paid for; the whole bill is not profit.
customers: Patients receive the care. The payer can be the household or another organisation covering the bill. An insurer or scheme can have agreed rates, documentation requirements and a payment timetable different from a patient paying directly.
drivers: Patients using the available services, staffed beds, the kind of care provided, doctor and nurse availability, the rates payers agree, running costs and how quickly bills are collected.

groups.title: Visits and tests without an overnight stay
groups.examples: Outpatient consultations, investigations and follow-up services.
groups.explanation: Outpatient means a patient is not admitted for an overnight hospital stay. The hospital earns for the relevant consultations or tests and pays for the people, supplies and equipment needed to deliver them.

groups.title: Hospital stays and intensive care
groups.examples: Inpatient admissions, intensive-care services and hospital stays.
groups.explanation: An inpatient is admitted to the hospital. Intensive care needs closer monitoring and the relevant specialist team and equipment. The number of beds is useful only alongside what services and staffing make them usable.

groups.title: Specialist medical and surgical services
groups.examples: Heart, brain and nerve, kidney, cancer, bone and joint, and other listed services.
groups.explanation: A specialty is an area of medical work. A directory shows which services a facility offers; it does not prove every hospital has the same capability or disclose a separate profit for each specialty.

groups.title: Women’s, children’s and other care
groups.examples: Maternity, children’s care, general adult medicine and related services where available.
groups.explanation: These involve different teams and patient needs. Check the particular hospital’s service list rather than assuming every service listed for the group is offered at every location.

basics.title: A bed has to be ready and staffed before it can be used
basics.text: An operational bed is one the hospital can actually use with the required people, equipment and permissions. Planned beds and installed beds are not necessarily usable beds.

basics.title: A bill and a payment can arrive at different times
basics.text: The hospital records services and sends a bill. An insurer or scheme may check the claim before paying. Money still owed by customers is called receivables; staff and suppliers may need payment while that bill remains unpaid.

steps.title: Prepare a usable hospital service
steps.text: Arrange premises, equipment, permissions and appropriately qualified doctors, nurses and support teams.

steps.title: Receive the patient and provide care
steps.text: Deliver a consultation, test, procedure or admission according to needs and the services the facility can provide.

steps.title: Record the work and bill the relevant payer
steps.text: The charges follow delivered services and the applicable patient or payer agreement. Insurance and scheme claims need the relevant supporting records.

steps.title: Collect payment and keep the hospital running
steps.text: Receive the money while paying teams and suppliers, maintaining equipment and funding any expansion.

specifics.title: A fuller hospital is a business measure, not proof of better care
specifics.text: Occupancy measures how much defined bed capacity is being used over time. Read its denominator and staffing. Higher occupancy alone does not establish patient outcomes or the quality of treatment.

specifics.title: Average revenue can change because the care changes
specifics.text: A longer stay, a more complex case or a different insurer agreement can change the average bill. Revenue per occupied bed is an average business measure, not the price charged to every patient.

specifics.title: A new hospital can have bills before it has many patients
specifics.text: New or acquired facilities need teams, local awareness and patient activity. Compare established sites with newer ones where the company provides that information, rather than treating every added bed as equally productive.

watch: Which beds and services are actually operating?
An expansion announcement is not a staffed service.
Read operational beds and hospitals already treating patients. Separate planned additions and newly acquired or managed sites, then compare patient activity and occupancy on the same basis.
Why has the average bill changed?
Different treatments and payer agreements affect averages.
Read the mix of consultations, admissions, procedures, length of stay and payer types. Check whether changes reflect a different service mix rather than the same treatment simply costing more.
Are teams and service systems keeping pace?
Expansion requires qualified people and dependable processes.

Read staffing, licences, accreditation and dated regulatory disclosures. Accreditation is an assessment against specified standards, not proof of every patient’s outcome; check which facility and period it covers.
Are delivered services being paid for?
Unpaid bills can use cash needed to run hospitals.

Compare amounts due from patients, insurers and schemes with collections and cash from operations. Look for how long bills are overdue and whether there are disputes, rather than assuming every unpaid bill is a loss.
Are new hospitals covering their ongoing costs?
Premises and staffing need payment before patient activity matures.
Read expansion spending, purchase payments, leases and start-up costs. Compare newer and established hospitals where disclosed, including whether the company owns or only operates each site.
risks: Difficulty hiring or keeping qualified doctors and nurses can limit the services and beds a hospital can use.
Care or rule failures cause disruption
Safety, service and regulatory problems can lead to claims, restrictions and extra costs.
Payers change rates or pay late
Lower agreed rates, disputed bills or slow insurer and scheme payments can affect earnings and cash.
New sites take longer to become busy
Rent, staff and other costs can continue while a new hospital builds patient activity.
context: Owning a hospital building and running it are different

On 16 September 2026, a Park subsidiary agreed to run an existing 300-bed hospital in Kanpur for 28 years. Axis Educational Society keeps ownership of the land and building. Park will pay for renovation and medical equipment and run the hospital; in return, it pays the owner a share of the money collected from patients, with a minimum monthly amount. The agreement takes effect no later than 1 April 2027, after renovation, so it does not yet add patients to Park’s network. Separately, on 26 August 2026 Park won a public–private partnership (PPP) mandate, an agreement with a government body, to build a 550-bed hospital in Prayagraj over about two years and then run it under a 45-year lease. Keep track of which sites Park owns, which it only runs, and which are already treating patients.
quiz: Would adding beds alone prove hospital earnings will rise?
No. Beds need staff, equipment, permissions and appropriate patient activity. Payments for the services also have to cover the associated costs.
sources: Kanpur operation-and-management agreement · exchange filing 16 September 2026

financialNotes.title: The table is the healthcare group, not a specialty ranking
financialNotes.text: The existing verified snapshot reports consolidated healthcare revenue and profit after tax. It does not show whether cardiology, oncology or a particular hospital earns the most.

financialNotes.title: Profit and cash answer different questions
financialNotes.text: Read the stated group and tax basis, then check receivables, operating cash flow, capital expenditure and lease or other commitments before concluding how much money is available after expansion.
